docs.title: Nestbox
docs.text: One bootable Ubuntu image that turns any machine — or any GPU cloud VM — into a governed workspace for AI agents.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
• Roadmap — what exists today and in which order it grows
  • API — authentication, errors, streaming
  • AI firewall — the policy model in practice
  • Models and hardware — what runs where
  • Claims — every number with its source

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
Running an agent stack is normally forty commands, six config files and a firewall written by hand. Nestbox reduces that to one boot, one web UI and one API — while keeping the isolation and the policy engine that make running agents safe at all.

Django is the control plane. NVIDIA OpenShell is the runtime. The appliance is the packaging.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
1. A claim without a row here does not ship.
  2. Comparisons against proprietary models are quoted, with a timestamp and a video link, never asserted in our own voice.
  3. VRAM figures are labelled as our estimates, because the vendor publishes none.
  4. Trademarked product names of other vendors are not used in comparative claims.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
Phase Content Done when 0 — Spike OpenShell on Ubuntu, headless, real VM (not WSL2) a script prints green 1 — Foundation Django, DRF, Swagger/Redoc, auth, inventory, live map, i18n, CI every container visible and controllable 2 — Sandboxes SDK adapter, CRUD, templates, exec, logs, ports create/enter/stop/delete a nest 3 — Policies structured editors, network rules, global policy, diff, rollback a rule change affects a running nest 4 — Agent packs schema, registry, first-party packs, wizard a chosen agent gets a working URL 5 — Network traffic container, WireGuard, CoreDNS, ACME, proxy routes https://<nest>.apps.<domain> with a valid cert 6 — ISO recipe → cloud-init → livefs → first boot → QEMU test one click produces a bootable ISO 7 — Backup restic targets, snapshots, single-file restore restore works from the browser

Current state: Phase 1. The data model and interfaces for later phases exist; the ISO renderer (recipe → autoinstall + seed) is implemented and tested.

docs.title: Language
docs.text:
English is the source language. There is no locale/en/ catalog: msgids are the English strings. Every user-visible string goes through {% translate %} or gettext, so a translation is data, not a code change.

Never translate: error.code values, enum values, log lines, policy YAML keys, pack keys, identifiers, docstrings.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• ruff and mypy are the authority; the CI runs both.
  • Docstrings in Google style, in English.
  • No silent except: — catch the narrowest type and either handle it or re-raise.
  • Every mutating API action writes an AuditEvent.

docs.title: Units
docs.text:
• timestamps: ISO 8601, UTC in the API, localized in the UI
  • sizes: integer bytes
  • durations: integer milliseconds
  • no localized numbers in machine-readable output

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
• decorative assets come from render_image; informational diagrams come from Mermaid sources
  • no text inside generated images; labels come from the diagram layer
  • no third-party logos or wordmarks
  • prompts are committed in assets/prompts/ so every asset is reproducible

docs.title: Commits
docs.text: Conventional Commits, English, imperative: feat(policies): hot-reload network rules. Sign off with git commit -s (DCO). No CLA.

docs.title: API
docs.text: Nestbox is the control plane of a one-boot AI appliance. It wraps the NVIDIA OpenShell gateway, so you manage sandboxes ("nests"), their policies, their reachable endpoints and the appliance itself through one HTTP API instead of a CLI.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text:
Two schemes are accepted on every endpoint:

  • Token — Authorization: Token <key>. Create one with POST /api/v1/identity/tokens/ (email and password), or in the UI under Account → API tokens. Revoke a token to cut off exactly one client.
  • Session — the browser cookie used by the web UI.

docs.title: Authorization
docs.text: Three roles exist: admin, operator, viewer. Each operation in this document carries x-roles (who may call it) and x-effect (read, write or destructive), so a client can render or hide actions without guessing.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Every failure uses one envelope, including streaming endpoints:

{"error": {"code": "sandbox.not_found", "message": "Nest 'x' does not exist.", "details": {}, "request_id": "…"}}

code is stable and safe to branch on. message is English and for developers; the UI translates the code, never the message.

docs.title: Streaming
docs.text: Endpoints marked x-stream: sse emit Server-Sent Events. Event names are part of the contract (containers, sandboxes, build-log), and each event's data is JSON.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text: /api/v1/ is frozen: breaking changes get a new prefix. /api/schema/v1/ is the machine-readable contract for it, and CI fails when the committed contract changes without intent.

docs.title: Sizing table
docs.text:
Model Checkpoint Weights (estimate) Fits on Nemotron Nano 12B v2 VL BF16 / FP8 ~26 GB / ~14 GB RTX 4090 24 GB, RTX 5090 32 GB Nemotron 3 Nano FP8 / NVFP4 ~32 GB / ~18 GB RTX 5090 32 GB, L40S 48 GB Nemotron 3 Super NVFP4 / BF16 ~65–70 GB / ~240 GB A100 80 GB, H100 80 GB, RTX PRO 6000 96 GB Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 / BF16 ~280–300 GB / ~1.1 TB 4× RTX PRO 6000, DGX B200, clustered DGX Spark

These numbers are our own arithmetic — roughly 0.55 bytes × parameters for NVFP4 weights plus activations and KV cache. NVIDIA does not publish a VRAM table for these checkpoints. Measure before you buy, and treat this page as a starting point rather than a guarantee.

docs.title: DGX Spark
docs.text:
A GB10 machine with 128 GB of unified memory and NVFP4 throughput in the petaflop class is the natural single-box target for Nemotron 3 Nano and, with a capped context, Super. It is not a single-node target for Ultra.

The appliance runs on it unchanged: same ISO, same UI, same policies. The only difference is that the local-nemotron pack has a GPU to attach to, so the provider profile can point at localhost.

docs.title: No GPU at all
docs.text: Nothing breaks. Use cloud models, keep the policies identical, and move the provider profile to a local endpoint when the hardware arrives. That is the recommended way to evaluate the workflow before spending money.

docs.title: ISO pipeline
docs.text: The build turns a recipe into a bootable Ubuntu Server image that is already configured for the operator who will use it.

docs.title: Stages
docs.text:
1. Discover — resolve the newest point release of the chosen LTS, verify SHA256SUMS and the GPG signature. A cached base image is reused when the hash matches.
  2. Render — the recipe becomes autoinstall.yaml (subiquity: identity, network, storage, packages, late commands) plus a NoCloud seed (user-data, meta-data) written to /cdrom/nocloud/. autoinstall is injected into the kernel command line.
  3. Bake — livefs-editor mutates a copy of the ISO: squashfs layers, the OpenShell binary, the controller image reference, agent images, the gateway seed, and the driver packages.
  4. First boot — netplan from the recipe, resolver, TLS material, stack start, gateway registration, preseed nest, self-check report.
  5. Verify — xorriso review, GRUB check, a QEMU boot with a marker string, then SHA256, SBOM and provenance.
  6. Publish — artifact, hash and log are linked in the UI.

docs.title: Honest timing
docs.text: A fully unattended Ubuntu install including squashfs extraction and NVIDIA drivers takes 5–15 minutes. The target is under ten minutes to the first running nest. "Two minutes" is achievable only after the installer has finished. Optimisation comes after measurement, not before.

docs.title: Secrets
docs.text: An ISO never contains plaintext credentials. It carries an encrypted envelope and a public key; the operator unlocks it at first boot, or enters the value in the UI. Afterwards the secret lives in an OpenShell provider profile, where the agent receives credentials without seeing them.

docs.title: Model weights
docs.text: Never shipped. The Nemotron licence is not Apache-2.0, so weights are pulled at runtime.

docs.title: Proxmox and QEMU test log
docs.text: This page records what has actually been executed on hardware, so a reader can tell a verified statement from an expectation.

docs.title: Environment
docs.text: Item Value Proxmox VE 9.2.21, node pve02, local-btrfs for disks, local for ISO images QEMU 11.0.3 (the same binary Proxmox uses) Test guest 4 GB RAM, 2 vCPU, 60 GB disk, VirtIO NIC on a user-mode network with DHCP Base image ubuntu-24.04-live-server-amd64.iso Nestbox image nestbox-24.04-slim.iso, 3151 MiB, SHA-256 34c76c4f516526f6c3e5733997c2264892e20e1fedfd1db7c9200ca9beb98db7

docs.title: What is verified
docs.text:
Step Result Remaster with xorriso -boot_image any replay ok — El Torito BIOS and UEFI entries preserved Seed embedded (/user-data, /meta-data, /nocloud/*, volume label cidata) ok Payload embedded (/nestbox.tar.gz, 2.3 MB) ok GRUB linux line patched with autoinstall ds=nocloud ok Unattended install, no question asked ok — reboot after 236 s Installed system boots, cloud-final finishes without failure ok nestbox-firstboot.service present and enabled by the installer ok First boot installs Docker, writes /etc/nestbox/nestbox.env, creates the certificate ok Controller image builds inside the guest and starts ok — PostgreSQL healthy, controller up UI answers on the configured port (443) with the self-signed certificate ok — HTTP 302 to /accounts/login/ Sign-in with the generated administrator account ok Dashboard reads the Docker socket ok — both containers listed as running

The same sequence was repeated on Proxmox VE with a VM created through the web UI (VM 210, 4 GB, 2 cores, 60 GB on local-btrfs, ISO attached as ide2), which is the walkthrough in the install guide.

docs.title: The four load-bearing details
docs.text:
Each of these cost a failed install cycle. They are the reason the build script looks the way it does.

  1. The autoinstall document must be nested in the seed's user-data. A sibling autoinstall.yaml on the ISO is ignored and subiquity silently falls back to the interactive installer. The document therefore lives under autoinstall: inside /user-data.
  2. GRUB ends a command at an unquoted ;. The datasource is passed as ds=nocloud and found through the cidata volume label instead of ds=nocloud;s=/cdrom/nocloud/.
  3. The payload's late-commands belong in user-data as well, not in autoinstall.yaml. With them in the wrong file the payload was copied but nestbox-firstboot.service was never enabled.
  4. The installer must not need a package mirror. Only openssh-server comes from the ISO pool; everything else is installed on first boot, with retries.

All late-commands are written as … || true: one failing command must never abort an otherwise good install.

docs.title: Runtime defects this test found
docs.text:
These only appear after the install, when the controller starts for the first time:

Symptom Cause Fix collectstatic fails: KeyError: 'NESTBOX_SECRET_KEY' the production settings require the runtime secret at image build time the build layer passes a throwaway key ModuleNotFoundError: unfold the admin theme was used but never declared django-unfold is a dependency ModuleNotFoundError: fido2 allauth's MFA URLs are mounted, but the extra was missing django-allauth[mfa] gunicorn: PermissionError on key.pem the container runs as uid 10001, the key was 0600 root first boot hands the pair to 10001 dashboard: runtime.unavailable uid 10001 is not in the Docker socket's group first boot records the host's Docker GID, compose adds the group unstyled sign-in page allauth's default templates branded account/login.html and account/logout.html

docs.title: Reproduce it without Proxmox
docs.text:
Any Linux host with KVM, xorriso and qemu-img can run the same test:

./scripts/iso/build_iso.sh \
  --base ubuntu-24.04-live-server-amd64.iso \
  --out  dist/nestbox-24.04-slim.iso \
  --seed dist/seed \
  --payload dist/nestbox.tar.gz

qemu-img create -f qcow2 /tmp/nestbox.qcow2 60G
qemu-system-x86_64 -m 4096 -smp 2 -cpu host -enable-kvm \
  -drive file=/tmp/nestbox.qcow2,if=virtio,format=qcow2 \
  -cdrom dist/nestbox-24.04-slim.iso \
  -display none -serial file:/tmp/install.log -no-reboot

The install is done when /tmp/install.log ends with reboot: Restarting system. Boot the disk again, and follow /var/log/nestbox/firstboot.log until it prints [nestbox] first boot complete together with the URL and the generated administrator password.

docs.title: Not covered yet
docs.text:
• Real hardware, and Proxmox with a physical NIC trunk or VLAN tags.
  • Ubuntu 22.04 and 26.04 base images (the seed format is the same, the ISOs are untested).
  • ACME certificates; the appliance ships with a self-signed pair and the TLS app has a certbot wrapper, but no public domain has been exercised end to end.

docs.title: Nemotron models
docs.text:
Only Nemotron is supported as a first-party local model. That is a deliberate product decision: one model family means one set of provider profiles, one set of policy profiles, and one thing to test.

Model Parameters Context Notes Nemotron Nano 12B v2 VL 12.6B dense 128K vision: up to 5 images, documents, video Nemotron 3 Nano 30B-A3B (3.2B active) 1M fastest in the family, hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE Nemotron 3 Super 120B-A12B 1M multi-agent and coding; 85.6 % PinchBench (OpenClaw) Nemotron 3 Ultra 550B-A55B 1M strongest open model in the family, NVFP4

Sources and dates are in ../claims.md.

docs.title: How a nest reaches a model
docs.text:
Nestbox never injects a model endpoint into an agent's code. It registers a provider profile and attaches it to the nest:

  • Cloud — a NIM endpoint on build.nvidia.com, or any OpenAI-compatible provider.
  • Local — a local-nemotron nest running vLLM, reachable over the overlay at http://<overlay-ip>:8000/v1.
  • Your laptop — the same thing, on your laptop, over WireGuard.

The policy does not change between these. What changes is one profile.

docs.title: VRAM guidance
docs.text:
See ../hardware/ for the sizing table and the caveats. The short version:

  • 12B VL → 24–32 GB VRAM
  • 3 Nano → 32–48 GB
  • 3 Super → 80 GB
  • 3 Ultra → 4× 96 GB or a DGX B200

Context length is the hidden cost: a 1M-token window needs hundreds of GB of KV cache, so cap the context on single-GPU deployments (32K–128K is the practical default) unless the hardware is sized for more.

docs.title: AI firewall for agent traffic
docs.text: A sandbox without a network policy is a machine with your API keys and an open route to anywhere. Nestbox gives every nest a policy document with four sections, and shows them as one firewall.

docs.title: The four sections
docs.text:
Section Fixed at What it controls filesystem_policy nest creation which paths are readable, writable, or both (include_workdir) landlock nest creation how strictly Landlock is applied (strict or best_effort) process nest creation the user and group the workload runs as network_policies live which binaries may reach which endpoints, with which methods

Only the network section is hot-reloadable. That is a property of the runtime, not a limitation we invented: filesystem and process boundaries cannot change under a running process without restarting it. The UI says so instead of pretending otherwise.

docs.title: A rule
docs.text:
network_policies:
  model-api:
    endpoints:
      - host: api.anthropic.com
        port: 443
        protocol: rest
        enforcement: enforced
        access: allow
        methods: [GET, POST]
    binaries:
      - path: /usr/local/bin/claude
  • enforcement: enforced blocks; audit records the attempt and allows it while you are building a policy.
  • binaries is the allow-list: only these executables may use the endpoint. A shell script that calls curl is not the binary, and is therefore not allowed.
  • access: deny is useful to carve exceptions out of a broad allow block.

docs.title: The workflow the UI gives you
docs.text:
1. Open a policy, edit the rule in a structured form or as YAML.
  2. Validate against the schema before anything is sent.
  3. Diff against the effective policy the gateway currently enforces.
  4. Apply — the gateway reloads the network section; existing keep-alive tunnels are closed at the reload boundary.
  5. Roll back to any earlier revision. Every save creates one.

The global policy is an administrator override: while active it replaces per-nest policies and blocks further per-nest edits. Deleting it restores normal selection.
